title: Strain-rate-dependent compressive behaviour and constitutive modelling of circular WAAM ER70S-6 steel walls
abstract: Abstract Circular collars and wall-type components fabricated using wire-arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) are increasingly being considered for load-bearing steel applications. However, detailed compressive properties and constitutive models are limited. In this study, a circular ER70S-6 steel wall of five layers deposited on the SS400 substrate by WAAM was explored to understand the microstructure-property relationship under compressive loading. The as-deposited wall had a microstructure consisting primarily of ferrite and pearlite. It also showed qualitatively observed scattered gas pores and a high proportion of high-angle grain boundaries (approximately 72%) in the load-bearing region. In contrast, the fusion zone at the wall-substrate interface had coarser grains. The hardness distribution in the wall showed a uniform value (200–235 HV), with a localized minimum in the fusion zone, followed by a recovery in the heat-affected zone and substrate. Quasi-static compression tests were performed at strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ using cylindrical specimens. Under quasi-static compression, the circular wall showed 0.2% yield strengths of 368.3 ± 20.2 to 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa and ultimate compressive strengths of 729.0 ± 31.2 to 801.7 ± 56.2 MPa across the strain rates, with mild strain-rate sensitivity and work-hardening capacities of 0.93–1.15. The flow curves of the wall material analyzed using the Hollomon, Ludwik, Swift, and Afrin models confirmed the high work-hardening capacity and stable constitutive equation values over the strain rates, dominated by a high-angle grain boundary microstructure.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a compelling method for fabricating near-net-shape structural components, offering a diminished buy-to-fly ratio and increased design flexibility compared with traditional subtractive and forming techniques. Wire-arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) is notably appealing for producing large components from steel, aluminum, and titanium because it integrates conventional arc-welding power sources and wire feedstock, achieving high deposition rates (frequently several kilograms per hour) while maintaining relatively low equipment costs [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. These attributes render WAAM a viable substitute for forging, casting, or plate-welded production of low- to medium-complexity components in industries such as construction, maritime, offshore, and energy infrastructure [ 6 ,  7 ,  8 ,  9 – 10 ].

Low-carbon and low-alloy steels have emerged as some of the most prevalent material systems in WAAM, owing to their durability, cost-effectiveness, and well-defined structural design principles. ER70S-6 is a widely utilised solid wire in gas metal arc welding, having gained significant traction in WAAM. Its notable manganese and silicon levels facilitate the deoxidation of the weld pool and ensure stable transfer, while also offering a commendable balance of strength and ductility in the as-deposited condition [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ]. Rafieazad et al. [ 13 ] produced ER70S-6 low-carbon steel walls through WAAM, revealing primarily ferritic-pearlitic microstructures with yield strengths ranging from 430 to 460 MPa and elongations exceeding 20%, thereby illustrating the alloy’s appropriateness for structural WAAM applications. Vahedi Nemani et al. [ 14 ] demonstrated that post-printing heat treatments specifically normalising and hardening can effectively homogenise the microstructure of WAAM ER70S-6, diminish anisotropy, and adjust the strength ductility balance. Complementary research on process optimisation, active cooling, and arc rotation has underscored the significance of ER70S-based consumables as essential alloys for the Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing of steel structures.

However, the microstructure-property relationships in WAAM steels are complicated owing to the repeated thermal cycling associated with layer-by-layer deposition. WAAM ER70S-6 walls typically comprise mixtures of columnar and equiaxed ferrite, intergranular pearlite, and, in some instances, martensitic or bainitic constituents, together with process-induced porosity and strong but spatially varying crystallographic textures [ 13 ,  15 ]. Electron backscatter diffraction studies revealed that as-deposited WAAM steels often possess high fractions of HAGBs superimposed onto a network of LAGBs, where HAGB-rich regions generally correspond to finer grains, greater hardness, and more isotropic mechanical response [ 13 ,  15 ]. Processing routes involving additional plastic deformation and recrystallisation, interpass rolling, or hybrid WAAM-rolling, for example, increase the fraction of HAGB and weaken the texture, improving the mechanical isotropy of both steels and refractory alloys [ 15 ,  16 ]. These observations underline that the grain boundary character, misorientation distributions, and hardness gradients are key descriptors when rationalising the performance of WAAM steels.

The few studies on the mechanical characterisation of WAAM steels have focused largely on tensile loading, often with the intention of deriving constitutive laws for structural analyses. As an example, tensile coupons were extracted from ER70S-6 walls by Rafieazad et al. [ 13 ] and fitted to classical Hollomon, Ludwik, and Swift hardening relationships that describe strain-hardening behaviour. Building on this work, Liu et al. [ 17 ] proposed tensile stress-strain models for WAAM carbon steels that account for process-induced inhomogeneity and provide improved predictive capability across a wide strain-rate range. Several groups have examined the high-temperature or dynamic response of additively manufactured steels and other alloys, observing that WAAM microstructures can display distinct strain-rate sensitivities and recovery behaviours relative to their wrought counterparts owing to their unique dislocation substructures and residual stresses [ 15 ,  16 ]. Nevertheless, systematic quasi-static compression data for as-built WAAM ER70S-6, especially at multiple strain rates, are still limited.

At the component level, WAAM is increasingly deployed for geometries that inherently operate under compressive or combined compressive-bending loads. Recent studies on WAAM steel tubular columns and concrete-filled WAAM tubes have demonstrated that, with appropriate design and post-processing, the axial compressive performance of WAAM members can approach that of conventional rolled or welded Sects [ 16 ,  18 ]. Applications envisaged for such members include bridge nodes, stiffeners, hollow columns, rings, and collars for attachment points and lifting lugs [ 3 ,  19 ]. In many of these cases, circular or annular geometries are preferred because they can distribute stresses more uniformly and minimise stress concentrations under compressive loading. However, most existing WAAM steel studies employ straight walls or prismatic blocks deposited on flat substrates; comparatively few investigations have examined circular walls or ring-shaped components fabricated directly by WAAM, despite their practical relevance in engineering design [ 3 ,  13 ].

These trends highlight several key knowledge gaps addressed in the present study. First, although the tensile behaviour of straight WAAM ER70S‑6 walls has been investigated, there is a lack of detailed microstructural and mechanical characterisation of circular WAAM steel components, especially those built from ER70S-6 feedstock. Second, whereas tensile properties and single-rate compression tests have been reported for WAAM ER70S-6 [ 13 ,  14 ], the effects of multi-strain rate quasi-static compression (10 − ⁴ − 10 − ¹ s − ¹) on circular WAAM ER70S-6 remain poorly quantified. In addition, no strain-rate-dependent compressive constitutive parameters are available for circular WAAM geometries. Third, few studies have explicitly linked EBSD-derived misorientation statistics and grain-boundary character to hardness gradients and compressive strain-hardening behaviour in WAAM low-carbon steels [ 15 ], so the microstructure-mechanics linkage under compression is largely unresolved.

This study addresses these gaps by processing a five-layer circular wall of ER70S-6 low-carbon steel on an SS400 structural steel substrate using a robotic gas metal arc WAAM system and systematically analysing its microstructure and compressive properties. A ring-shaped wall with a height of approximately 10 mm was deposited in a closed circular path, and cylindrical compression specimens with a diameter of 4 mm and a height of 6 mm were machined from the centre area of the wall to reduce the influence of substrate dilution and edge effects. Comprehensive microstructural analyses using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and EBSD were conducted on the cross-sectional areas, including the deposited wall, fusion zone, heat-affected zone, and substrate. Vickers microhardness mapping was used to capture the hardness gradient from the top layer to the substrate. Quasi-static compression tests were performed at room temperature with strain rates of 1 × 10⁻⁴, 1 × 10⁻³, 1 × 10⁻², and 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. The obtained stress-strain curves were analysed to obtain the yield strength, ultimate compressive strength, strain-hardening exponent, and hardening ability. Based on these results, this study attempts to interpret the structure-property relationships that control the load-bearing capability of circular WAAM ER70S-6 components using EBSD-based misorientation distributions and LAGB/HAGB fractions coupled with hardness and multi-rate compressive properties. Experimental data required for the design and qualification of ring-like WAAM steel parts operating under compressive loading are also provided.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The experiments were carried out using a robotic gas metal arc wire-arc additive manufacturing (GMA-WAAM) system configured to deposit a circular wall of ER70S-6 low-carbon steel on an SS400 structural steel substrate. The WAAM cell, schematically illustrated in Fig.  1 , consisted of a six-axis KUKA KR 16 KS industrial robot equipped with a GMAW torch, integrated with a Megmeet Artsen Plus 350QR power source and a KR-C2 controller for precise path planning. A high-purity argon shielding gas (99.99%) was supplied at a controlled flow rate, and the substrate plate was rigidly clamped onto a steel worktable beneath the robot torch.

Pure argon (99.99%) was used as the shielding gas. Ar-CO₂ or Ar-O₂ mixtures are commonly used in conventional GMAW/MAG of ER70S-6 steel. However, the present study used pulsed GMA-WAAM. An argon-rich atmosphere is generally preferred for stable spray or pulsed-spray transfer in ferrous alloys. Resende et al. [ 20 ] showed that shielding-gas composition strongly affects the globular-to-spray transition current and transfer stability for ER70S-6 wire. Higher CO₂ contents increase the transition current and can affect transfer regularity. Therefore, pure Ar was selected to maintain stable pulsed transfer and reduce additional oxidation during multi-layer deposition. This is consistent with the high-purity or argon-rich shielding adopted in other ER70S-6 WAAM studies [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ].

Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the robotic GMA-WAAM configuration utilised for the fabrication of the circular ER70S-6 wall. The inset demonstrates the GMA-WAAM process utilised in the deposition of the circular wall

The feedstock was a solid ER70S-6 welding wire with a nominal diameter of 1.2 mm, whereas the base material was SS400 structural steel. The nominal chemical compositions of the filler and substrate are listed in Table  1 , and their room-temperature tensile properties are shown in Table  2 , showing that ER70S-6 provides slightly higher strength and ductility compared with SS400 and is metallurgically compatible as a WAAM consumable [ 13 ,  14 ].

Table 1 Chemical Composition of ER70S-6 wire and substrate (wt%) Element ER70S-6 (wt%) SS400 (wt%) Carbon, C 0.09 0.14 Manganese, Mn 1.65 0.705 Phosphorus, P 0.012 0.009 Sulfur, S 0.018 0.007 Silicon, Si 0.95 0.255 Copper, Cu 0.35 0.006
Table 2 Mechanical properties of ER70S-6 wire and substrate Materials Tensile strength (MPa) Elongation (%) ER70S-6 480 22 SS400 400 17

Throughout the build process, the parameters were kept constant to ensure stable and repeatable deposition conditions. The welding current was set to 150 A, travel speed to 400 mm/min, and argon flow rate to 15 L/min, as summarised in Table  3 . The selected values were derived from early trials aimed at generating continuous beads with sufficient fusion, while minimising excessive heat input and distortion, consistent with the parameter ranges previously documented for the WAAM of low-carbon steels. The net heat input was calculated as Q = η·U·I/v, where η is the arc thermal efficiency, U the arc voltage, I the welding current, and v the travel speed in mm/s. An efficiency of η = 0.8 was used, which is the value commonly adopted for GMAW [ 3 ,  20 ,  22 ,  24 ].

Table 3 Deposition parameters Process Parameters Value (unit) Welding Current (I) 150 (A) Voltage (U) 20 V Travel speed 400 (mm/min) Wire Feed Speed 4.5 m/min Contact-tip-to-workpiece distance (CTWD) 15 mm Metal transfer mode Pulsed transfer Net Heat input 360 J/mm Interlayer Dwell Time 90 s Shielding gas 99.99% Argon gas Wire deposition ER70S-6 steel Wire diameter 1.2 (mm) Substrate SS400 steel Gas flow rate 15 (L/min) Number of passes per layer 1

Deposition was performed in a closed circular path: the robot torch was programmed to trace a circular trajectory in the X-Y plane while incrementally stepping in the Z-direction to build up the height. A schematic of the circular geometry of the deposited wall with a microhardness schematic and compression specimen is shown in Figs.  2  (a), (b), and (c), respectively. The arc start and stop points were kept at the same angular position for every layer. A short and repeatable overlap was used at this seam. This helped reduce the start-end height mismatch and produced a closed ring. One circular pass was used for each layer. A dwell time of 90 s was applied between layers. Thermal control was achieved passively. The SS400 substrate was clamped to a large steel fixture. The fixture acted as a passive heat sink and helped reduce warping and distortion.

Fig. 2 Schematic of the sample geometry and extraction from the WAAM-fabricated circular wall: ( a ) printed circular wall on the SS400 substrate showing locations of microstructural, microhardness, and compression specimens; ( b ) cross-section used for microhardness mapping along the build direction; and ( c ) cylindrical compression specimen with the loading axis parallel to the build direction

Specimens for metallography, microhardness, and compression tests were extracted after deposition using wire-cut EDM to minimise thermal damage. Cross-sections containing the deposited wall and underlying substrate were cut normal to the build direction, as indicated in Fig.  2 (b). The specimens were ground with SiC papers from 320 to 4000 grit and polished with a colloidal silica suspension to obtain a deformation-free surface. Final surface quality for EBSD was further improved by electrolytic polishing in a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid in ethanol at 15 V for 10 s. For general phase and morphology observations, the polished samples were etched in a 4% Nital solution for 4 s and examined using optical microscopy and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

Vickers microhardness measurements were also performed on the same polished cross-sections to characterise the hardness gradient from the top of the circular wall to the substrate. A microhardness tester was used with a load of 1 kgf and a dwell time of 10 s, and indents were placed along the build direction at a spacing of approximately 0.5 mm starting from the top surface of the wall, traversing all five deposited layers, the fusion zone, the partially melted zone, the heat-affected zone, and into the SS400 base metal. The layout of the hardness traverses is shown schematically in Fig.  2 (b), where the measurement line is aligned with the wall height and passes through the wall-substrate interface region. This arrangement allows a direct correlation of hardness variations with the different metallurgical zones generated by the WAAM thermal cycles.

Cylindrical specimens for quasi-static compression tests were machined from the central region of the deposited wall, as shown in Fig.  2  (c). This sampling strategy was adopted in order to avoid regions very close to the substrate and the top free surface, so that the influence of chemical dilution and extreme thermal gradients on the measured properties could be minimised. The cylinders had an initial diameter D₀ = 4 mm and height H₀ = 6 mm, giving a height-to-diameter ratio H₀/D₀ = 1.5 within the range recommended by the compression testing standards for metallic materials to avoid excessive buckling and end constraints [ 25 ]. Similar 4 mm × 6 mm cylindrical specimens have been used in other quasi-static compression studies of metallic alloys [ 26 ,  27 ], supporting the suitability of this geometry for an accurate compressive characterisation. The loading axis of each specimen was parallel to the build direction, such that the measured response reflected the through-thickness behaviour of the circular wall.

Compression tests were performed at room temperature using a servo-electric universal testing machine (Instron 3369) according to the general procedures of ASTM E9 [ 25 ]. Nominal engineering strain rates of 1 × 10⁻⁴, 1 × 10⁻³, 1 × 10⁻², and 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ were imposed by adjusting the crosshead speed. In order to minimise the friction between the specimen ends and the compression platens, a thin layer of Vaseline was applied to the loading faces before testing. Three nominally identical specimens were evaluated for each strain rate, and the reported 0.2% offset yield strength, ultimate compressive strength, and work‑hardening capacity represented the mean values, with standard deviations calculated to assess repeatability.

sections.heading: Macroscopic morphology of the circular WAAM wall
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the typical macroscopic appearance of the WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular wall. Figure  3 (a) shows the side view of the as-built wall on the SS400 substrate. Figure  3 (b) shows the top view along the build direction. Figure  3 (c) shows the etched cross-sectional macrograph of the wall-substrate assembly. These images show the as-built geometry, the layer-by-layer stacking sequence, and the surface quality of the circular wall.

Fig. 3 Macroscopic morphology of the WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular wall on SS400 substrate: ( a ) side view of the as-built circular wall, ( b ) top view along the build direction, and ( c ) etched cross-sectional macrograph showing continuity at the wall-substrate interface and the annular cross-section of the deposited wall with five layers (total height of 10 mm with 10 mm wall thickness)

From the dimensional annotations in Fig.  3 , the circular wall exhibits a nominal outer diameter of 40 mm, a wall thickness of 10 mm, and a build height of 10 mm. With five deposited layers, the mean layer height was approximately 2 mm per layer, consistent with the typical layer heights reported for ER70S-6 WAAM walls fabricated with comparable heat input and travel speed [ 13 ,  21 ]. The resulting height-to-thickness ratio (height/thickness = 1) places the ring in a relatively stocky regime, which is favourable for avoiding macroscopic buckling during subsequent quasi-static compression testing [ 16 ,  18 ].

Figure  3 (a) confirms that the side -view morphology of the deposited wall follows the intended circular tool path with good dimensional accuracy. There was no obvious start-stop gap in the ring, and it appeared fully closed, which suggests that both the robot path and arc re-striking were well controlled. Similar degrees of path fidelity have been reported for WAAM steel tubes and rings when closed trajectories are used, and robotic synchronisation is carefully calibrated [ 16 ,  28 ]. In the present case, there is no evidence of any macroscopic misalignment or step at the overlap region at the scale of Fig.  3 (a), which indicates that any remnant of the start-end overlap is small compared to the wall thickness.

Figure  3 (b) shows that the top surface of the wall is slightly convex, which is typical for WAAM beads owing to the surface tension and partial re-melting of the underlying layers, leading to the formation of the bead crown. There was no severe underfill or overfill as would be expected from sharp ridges, large depressions, or gross collapse of the top bead. In conjunction with the constant measured height of 10 mm, this indicates that the selected process parameters provided a stable melt pool and roughly constant reinforcement by layer, aligning with earlier ER70S-6 WAAM studies identifying similar operating parameter windows for stable wall building [ 13 ,  21 ].

Further evidence of the integrity of the wall and the wall-substrate interface can be seen in the cross-sectional macrograph in Fig.  3 (c). The cross-section of the wall shows the ER70S-6 deposit, fusion zone, and SS400 substrate after etching. The interface between the deposit and substrate was continuous and fully fused for the entire observed circumference, with no lack-of-fusion or keyhole-like defects. Consistent with other ER70S-6 WAAM studies on steel substrates, good metallurgical bonding and smooth interface morphology have been reported for comparable heat-input conditions [ 22 ,  29 ]. The fusion boundary in Fig.  3 (c) is gently curved owing to the circular geometry and radial heat flow during deposition and is free from obvious macro-cracks or delamination.

Overall, the macrostructural examination in Fig.  3  shows that the circular ER70S-6 wall was fabricated with good geometric consistency, full macroscopic fusion to the SS400 substrate, and without gross defects. The dimensions of the wall (40 mm diameter, 10 mm thickness, and 10 mm height) and the visually uniform layer stacking provide a good basis for extracting representative cylindrical compression specimens from the central region and interpreting the subsequent microstructure and mechanical-property data as intrinsic to the WAAM-deposited material rather than being dominated by obvious macroscopically visible flaws. This combination of a realistic geometry in the form of a circle together with macroscopically sound build quality positions the current specimen as a relevant benchmark for WAAM-produced ring-like or tubular components intended for compressive and multi-axial loading in structural applications [ 16 ,  18 ,  28 ].

sections.heading: Microstructure of the interface of the deposited wall and substrate
paragraphs: SEM was performed to examine the microstructure near the wall-substrate interface, as shown in Fig.  4 . The top part of Fig.  4 (a) corresponds to the WAAM deposited ER70S-6 wall close to the interface region, whereas the bottom part of Fig.  4 (b) shows the FZ, PMZ, HAZ, and SS400 base.
Fig. 4 SEM images near the wall-substrate interface of the WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular wall: ( a ) Deposited wall region, and ( b ) Substrate

In the as-deposited wall region, Fig.  4 (a), the matrix is primarily ferritic with a network of pearlite colonies that decorate the prior austenite grain boundaries and local interdendritic regions. The ferrite is mainly polygonal/equiaxed in morphology, with bands of pearlite aligned along microsegregated regions, which is typical for ER70S-6 low-carbon steel that has solidified under moderate cooling rates and then undergone repeated thermal cycling in the WAAM process [ 13 ,  30 ]. Similarly, as-deposited WAAM ER70S-6 walls have been reported to consist of ferrite with colonies of pearlite of comparable characteristic size [ 31 ,  32 ]. The relatively fine ferrite-pearlite microstructure observed is consistent with the microhardness measured across the deposited wall (discussed in the upcoming section), which is higher than that of typical normalised C-Mn steels but within the range reported for as-deposited WAAM ER70S-6 [ 13 ,  22 ].

Small, nearly spherical gas pores are visible in the examined wall region of Fig.  4 (a), which are largely isolated and have diameters that are clearly smaller than the layer height. No large keyhole-type pores, wormholes, or interconnected porosity networks were observed. This morphology is in line with previous studies, where WAAM carbon steels produced with GMAW-based processes exhibited isolated rounded pores associated with shielding gas entrapment or unstable droplet transfer, but no gross porosity when the process window was optimised for stable arc operation [ 30 ,  31 ]. In similar ER70S-6 WAAM walls, pore volume fractions below 1–2% and pore sizes typically < 100 μm have been reported, with limited impact on static strength but potential implications for fatigue and fracture [ 22 ,  31 ]. Therefore, the pores observed in the SEM images are treated as qualitative microstructural features.

In Fig.  4 (b), the FZ and transition into the substrate are well-resolved. Immediately beneath the deposited wall, an etched band with a more complex morphology appears, associated with the FZ/PMZ, in which the ER70S-6 deposit and SS400 substrate are mixed and resolidified. In this area, the structure comprises partially columnar and partially equiaxed ferrite with pearlite, which is the result of solidification under a steep temperature gradient normal to the interface and several reheating processes from subsequent layers [ 22 ,  33 ].

Closer to the substrate, the FZ transitioned into a HAZ in the SS400 plate. The HAZ in Fig.  4 (b) can be subdivided into a coarse-grained region adjacent to the FZ and a finer-grained intercritical/subcritical HAZ extending into the substrate. Coarse-grained HAZ displays larger ferrite grains and more widely spaced pearlite colonies, which are characteristic of austenitisation and grain growth during high-temperature exposure near the fusion boundary, followed by transformation on cooling [ 30 ,  31 ]. Moving further into the substrate, the microstructure gradually returned to the typical morphology of hot-rolled SS400 with finer grains and a more uniform distribution of pearlite. These gradients of grain size and phase morphology along the FZ-HAZ-substrate direction are a direct consequence of the thermal field imposed by the circular WAAM path.

Additionally, Fig.  4 (b) shows no metallurgical discontinuities at the wall-substrate interface. The FZ appeared to be fully bonded to the substrate, and continuous dendritic/ferro-pearlitic structures across the nominal fusion line were clearly observed. Moreover, no unmelted islands, unbonded gaps, or continuous oxide layers were observed at the resolution of the SEM. This continuous microstructural transition strongly indicates sound metallurgical bonding between the ER70S-6 deposit and SS400 plate [ 22 ,  29 ].

The circular deposition path has an indirect but important function in determining the microstructure, as shown in Fig.  4 . In a ring shape, each circumferential pass is locally similar to a continuous straight bead, but its global heat flow is radially constrained by the relatively narrow wall and massive substrate ring. This tends to homogenise the cooling conditions along the circumference, reducing the variation in the microstructure around the ring compared with highly asymmetric geometries, while still promoting through-thickness gradients from the wall top to the substrate. Similar observations have been made in WAAM tubular or ring-like structures, where circumferential heat flow and repeated thermal cycling lead to reasonably uniform ferrite-pearlite morphologies along the hoop direction, with microstructural variation primarily in the radial and build directions [ 16 ,  18 ,  28 ].

sections.heading: EBSD crystallographic analysis
paragraphs: EBSD measurements were conducted at the centre of the circular WAAM wall to characterise the crystallographic texture, grain structure, and grain-boundary misorientation of the as-built ER70S-6 deposit. The resulting IPF orientation map, {001} pole Fig., and grain-boundary misorientation histogram are presented in Fig.  5 (a-c), respectively.

Fig. 5 EBSD characterisation at the centre of the WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular wall: ( a ) inverse pole Fig. (IPF) orientation map (build direction), ( b ) {001} pole Fig., and ( c ) grain-boundary misorientation distribution

Figure  5 (a) shows the IPF cube and orientation map displaying the crystallographic orientation of the grains in the analysed area, colour-coded according to the standard stereographic triangle for bcc ferrite. The map reveals a fine equiaxed ferrite-pearlite structure with a relatively heterogeneous distribution of colours, indicating that no single orientation dominates. There was no continuous band of similarly coloured grains aligned with the build direction, and the grain clusters with similar colours were small and dispersed. This behaviour reflects a weak global texture, in contrast to the strongly columnar and directionally solidified microstructures in which < 001 > or < 111 > fibre textures produce large domains of uniform colour aligned with the direction of heat flow or build [ 15 ,  34 ]. The weak texture observed here aligns with the ferrite-pearlite morphology shown in Fig.  4  and with earlier EBSD investigations on WAAM ER70S-6 and C-Mn steels, where repeated thermal cycling and partial recrystallisation break down strong as-solidified textures and yield more quasi-random orientation distributions [ 13 ,  31 ].

The corresponding {001} pole is shown in Fig.  5 (b), which confirms this assessment. The pole figure shows diffuse intensity clouds with only mild clustering and no sharp maxima, indicating that the multiples-of-random-distribution (MRD) values remained close to random (i.e., no strong, narrow texture components). In strongly textured WAAM or welded steels, {001} pole figures often display pronounced peaks along the build or transverse directions associated with < 001>//BD or other preferred orientations, sometimes exceeding 4–6 MRD [ 15 ,  32 ]. In contrast, the diffuse pattern suggests that texture strengthening is limited, and the mechanical response is unlikely to be dominated by a single crystallographic fibre. This is favourable for quasi-isotropic behaviour in compression, especially when combined with a high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries, as discussed below [ 16 ,  28 ].

The grain-boundary misorientation distribution in Fig.  5 (c) provides a more quantitative picture of the boundary character. Boundaries with misorientation angles < 2° were excluded as noise; boundaries in the range 2–15° were classified as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs), and those > 15° as high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), following the common EBSD practice for steels [ 35 ]. The histogram shows a prominent peak at low misorientation around 3–4°, followed by a broad distribution extending up to 60°. When integrated over the entire range, the LAGBs (2–15°) accounted for approximately 28% of the total boundary length, whereas the HAGBs (> 15°) contributed about 72%. Thus, the microstructure was strongly HAGB-dominated, with a relatively modest but non-negligible fraction of low-angle boundaries that likely corresponded to subgrain structures and recovered dislocation walls within the ferrite grains.

The histogram within the HAGB range displays extensive local maxima in the 30–45° interval and again around 55–60°, aligning with the crystallography of bcc ferrite, where specific misorientations linked to prevalent slip systems (< 111 > and < 110 > rotations) and former austenite grain boundaries may lead to favoured misorientation bands [ 36 ]. Comparable misorientation distributions-pronounced low-angle peaks at several degrees, a substantial high-angle grain boundary (HAGB) fraction exceeding 70%, and extensive peaks at intermediate and high angles have been reported for WAAM ER70S-6 and other low-carbon steels following successive thermal cycling and partial recrystallisation [ 13 ,  15 ,  31 ]. Specifically, Tankova et al. [ 31 ] quantified HAGB fractions of approximately 70–80% in CMT-WAAM C-Mn steel walls, whereas Panchenko et al. [ 15 ] reported HAGB fractions exceeding 80% in functionally graded HSLA steel produced via WAAM, both of which are linked to refined microstructures and relatively isotropic quasi-static characteristics.

The high fraction of HAGBs (72%) combined with a weak global texture is expected to promote quasi‑isotropic plasticity and sustained work hardening in compression, as confirmed by the subsequent strain‑rate‑dependent compression tests [ 37 ].

sections.heading: Microhardness distribution and structure-property correlation
paragraphs: Figure  6  illustrates the Vickers microhardness profile measured along the construction direction of the circular wall and into the SS400 substrate, accompanied by example SEM images at designated points. Indentations were created on a polished cross-section beginning at the upper surface of the WAAM wall, traversing the deposited area, crossing the wall-substrate interface, and penetrating into the base metal, with a nominal interval of approximately 0.5 mm between consecutive indents. This offers a one-dimensional representation of the variation in local hardness with depth within the circular structure.
Fig. 6 Vickers microhardness profile measured along the build direction from the top of the WAAM-deposited layer to the substrate

The hardness values in the deposited ER70S-6 wall were comparatively high and exhibited only slight variability. The upper and mid-wall regions mostly ranged from approximately 200 to 235 HV, with local peaks approaching 240–250 HV. A higher near-surface value was also observed at the top of the wall. Toward the lower deposited region, the hardness gradually decreased to approximately 170–195 HV before reaching the fusion-boundary trough. The observed hardness levels and distribution align with previously reported values for as-deposited WAAM low-carbon steels and ER70S-6 walls, which generally fall within the 200–260 HV range under similar process parameters and interpass temperatures [ 13 ,  21 ,  30 ,  31 ].

At the wall-substrate transition, the hardness profile showed a sharp local trough, with the minimum falling to approximately 100–150 HV in the fusion-boundary region. The adjacent PMZ/HAZ region then recovered to approximately 190–220 HV. The SEM image at this point in Fig.  6  reveals a more coarsely etched microstructure than that of the wall interior, indicative of significant thermal exposure in this area. The SEM qualitatively mirrored the hardness variations along the traverse. Regions in the upper and mid-wall, where the hardness remains in the 200–235 HV, with local peaks approaching 240–250 HV, show a comparatively finer ferrite-pearlite morphology, whereas the fusion/CGHAZ zone at the hardness minimum exhibits visibly coarser etched features. Further into the substrate, the microstructure became more typical of rolled SS400, consistent with the lower, nearly uniform hardness measured there. Comparable hardness depressions at the FZ/CGHAZ have been noted in both conventional welds and WAAM-fabricated carbon steels, where the localised thermal cycle markedly diverges from that of the deposited wall and the distant base metal [ 15 ,  30 ,  31 ].

Outside this interface region, within the heat-affected zone of the SS400 substrate, the hardness progressively increased from the minimum in the fusion zone and thereafter stabilised at lower levels typical of the base plate. Further into the substrate-side region, the hardness stabilised at approximately 190–205 HV, consistent with documented hardness levels for SS400 and comparable structural steels in the as-rolled state [ 32 ]. The comprehensive profile indicates a consistent decline in hardness from the upper wall to the substrate, punctuated by a distinct minimum at the FZ/CGHAZ, and subsequently transitioning to the lower, nearly uniform hardness of the base metal.

sections.heading: Strain-rate-dependent true stress-true strain behaviour
paragraphs: The true stress-true strain curves for the WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular wall, acquired at four quasi-static strain rates of 1 × 10⁻⁴, 1 × 10⁻³, 1 × 10⁻², and 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, are illustrated in Fig.  7 . All tests were conducted at ambient temperature on cylindrical specimens (4 mm diameter, 6 mm height) with the loading axis aligned with the build direction.
Fig. 7 True stress-true strain curves of WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 circular-wall specimens tested in compression at four quasi-static strain rates

All the strain rate curves exhibited comparable overall morphologies. An initial linear elastic area existed up to real stresses of roughly 0.002–0.003, succeeded by yielding and a gradual transition into plastic flow. The elastic slope indicates an effective Young’s modulus almost equivalent to that anticipated for low-carbon steel (200 GPa), affirming that no macroscopically dominant defect controlled the initial response. Beyond the onset of plasticity, the material exhibited continuous work hardening up to large compressive strains on the order of 0.25–0.40, with no evidence of abrupt strain softening or unstable localisation within the strain range investigated. This type of response is typical of dense WAAM steels under quasi-static loading [ 16 ,  38 ].

The curves showed a clear but moderate strain rate sensitivity across the four strain rates. As the strain rate increased from 1 × 10⁻⁴ to 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, the entire flow curve shifted upward: the onset of yielding occurred at a higher stress level, and the subsequent plastic flow was consistently higher at a given true strain. However, the overall shape of the curves remained similar, with no qualitative change in the yielding or work hardening characteristics. This behaviour is typical of low-carbon steels and WAAM-fabricated steels under quasi-static loading, where rate effects are present but modest and do not fundamentally alter the deformation mechanism [ 16 ,  38 ].

The plastic portions of the curves exhibited smooth, continuous work hardening up to relatively large compressive strains (on the order of 0.25–0.40), without any visible Lüders plateau, sharp softening, or serrated flow. The hardening rate progressively diminished with an increase in strain, which aligned with the expected behaviour of ductile ferritic steels. When analysed using conventional power-law descriptions, such as the Hollomon or Ludwik equations, the plastic segments yield strength coefficients and strain-hardening exponents that align with the ranges typically documented for WAAM normal-strength steels derived from ER70S-6 or comparable consumables [ 17 ,  21 ,  38 ].

At elevated strains, the curves depicted in Fig.  7  exhibit continued hardening, although at a diminished rate, until the end of the recorded data. The material does not exhibit a clear “densification plateau” similar to that observed in cellular or foam-like materials; instead, it functions as a dense, ductile metal characterised by a continuously increasing flow stress. The observed slight upturn or steepening of the curves at the highest strains for the faster tests is attributable to a combination of geometrical effects, specifically the barrelling of the short cylinders and the increasing constraint as the specimen flares against the platens. These phenomena are commonly observed in compression tests conducted on short steel cylinders [ 16 ,  39 ].

When comparing the four rates at a fixed strain, the separation between the curves was relatively modest and remained approximately parallel throughout most of the plastic regime. This observation supports the concept that rate hardening is primarily influenced by a strain-independent offset rather than a significant alteration in the work-hardening mode. This behaviour is consistent with general observations for low-carbon steels, where the quasi-static rate sensitivity is typically ascribed to thermally activated dislocation glide and moderate dynamic recovery effects [ 40 ,  41 ]. In the context of WAAM steels, the current findings are consistent with the stress-strain responses reported by Huang et al. [ 38 ]. Normal-strength WAAM steels produced using ER70S-6 or comparable wires demonstrated yield strengths ranging from 350 to 450 MPa and ultimate compressive or tensile strengths between 700 and 900 MPa, exhibiting only slight sensitivity to quasi-static rates [ 40 ,  41 ].

The compressive behaviour remained stable up to considerable strains (0.3–0.4) without indications of premature failure. This observation is promising for applications involving the local compressive loading of WAAM rings or collars [ 16 ,  42 ]. The analysis of hardness and microstructural observations, along with the flow curves, indicated that the as-built centre region of the circular wall exhibited the characteristics of ductile, moderately strengthening low-carbon steel. Its mechanical properties were comparable to or slightly exceeded those of conventional ER70S-6 weld metal.

sections.heading: Strain-rate-dependent compressive strength and constitutive modelling
paragraphs: Figure  8  summarises the evolution of the main compressive properties and work-hardening parameters of the circular WAAM ER70S-6 wall as a function of the quasi-static strain rate (10⁻⁴-10⁻¹ s⁻¹). The data were extracted from the true stress-true strain curves in Fig.  7  using a 0.2% offset definition of yield and fitting several classical work-hardening laws.

Fig. 8 Effect of strain rate on ( a ) Yield stress, ( b ) ultimate compressive stress, ( c ) hardening capacity, ( d ) strain hardening exponent, and ( e ) strength coefficient (strain hardening exponent and strength coefficient are evaluated using Ludwik, Hollomon, Swift, and Afrin et al. equations.)

The compressive properties are summarised in Table  4 . Both the 0.2% offset yield strength and ultimate compressive strength exhibited mild positive strain-rate sensitivity, with YS increasing from 368 ± 20 MPa at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 397 ± 3 MPa at 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, and UCS reaching a maximum of 802 ± 56 MPa at 10⁻² s⁻¹. The work-hardening capacity Hc remains consistently high (0.93–1.15), indicating robust strain-hardening across the quasi-static regime.

Table 4 Quasi-static compressive properties of the circular WAAM ER70S-6 wall at different strain rates (mean ± SD,  n  = 3) Strain rate (s⁻¹) Yield stress, YS (MPa) Ultimate compressive stress, UCS (MPa) Hardening capacity, Hc (–) UCS/YS (mean ratio) 1 × 10⁻⁴ 380.0 ± 37.8 729.0 ± 31.2 0.93 ± 0.14 1.92 1 × 10⁻³ 368.3 ± 20.2 735.0 ± 31.2 1.00 ± 0.13 2.00 1 × 10⁻² 375.0 ± 22.9 801.7 ± 56.2 1.15 ± 0.15 2.14 1 × 10⁻¹ 397.0 ± 2.6 783.7 ± 5.5 0.99 ± 0.05 1.97

From Fig.  8 (a) and Table  4 , the 0.2% offset yield strength (YS) of the WAAM wall ranged from 368.3 ± 20.2 to 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa across the four strain rates. At the lowest rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, YS is 380.0 ± 37.8, decreases slightly at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (368.3 ± 20.2), and then increases again to 375.0 ± 22.9 MPa at 10⁻² s⁻¹ and 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa at 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. Overall, the variation is modest, indicating a weak but positive rate sensitivity, with some non-monotonicity that is typical when local microstructural heterogeneity contributes to scatter in the onset of yielding. This behaviour indicates a positive, but relatively small, strain-rate sensitivity in the yield regime, consistent with previous observations on ferrite-pearlite steels and cast Al/Mg alloys, where m-values of the order of 0.01–0.03 have been reported over a similar quasi-static strain-rate window [ 43 ,  44 ].

These compressive yield stresses (368.3 ± 20.2 to 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa) are lower than the nominal tensile strength of the ER70S-6 wire (480 MPa in tension, Table  2 ) and significantly higher than the specified yield of SS400 (245–275 MPa in tension). Comparable YS levels (320–420 MPa in quasi-static compression) have been reported for WAAM-built ER70S-6 and low-carbon steel walls and blocks [ 15 ,  24 ,  44 ]. Such strength levels are generally associated with ferrite-pearlite microstructures, repeated thermal cycling, and work-hardened interlayer regions. In these studies, increasing the strain rate within the quasi-static regime also produced only mild strengthening, attributed to the limited rate dependence of dislocation glide at room temperature in bcc ferrite-dominated steels, provided that dynamic strain aging was not active. The slight dip in YS at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ in Fig.  8 (a) can be rationalised by the local grain-size variation and other microstructural heterogeneities sampled by the small compression specimens. The SEM images in Fig.  4  reveal isolated pores in the examined wall region, whereas the EBSD map in Fig.  5  shows a mixture of fine and coarser grains. The larger SD at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (Table  4 ) indicates that specimen-to-specimen heterogeneity is most pronounced at the lowest rate, consistent with the local microstructural variations observed by SEM/EBSD (Figs.  4  and  5 ).

Figure  8 (b) shows the ultimate compressive strength (UCS), defined as the maximum true stress reached before pronounced barreling or macroscopic instability. UCS values fall in the range 729.0 ± 31.2 to 801.7 ± 56.2 MPa over 10⁻⁴-10⁻¹ s⁻¹. The lowest rate (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) yielded UCS 729.0 ± 31.2 MPa, which increased to 735.0 ± 31.2 MPa at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and peaked at approximately 801.7 ± 56.2 MPa at 10⁻² s⁻¹, followed by a slight decrease at 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. This trend, an initial increase in UCS with strain rate followed by slight saturation, is consistent with classical strain-rate-sensitive metals, where dislocation drag increases at higher rates, raising the flow stress, while the microstructural relaxation mechanisms (e.g., dynamic recovery) do not fully counteract this effect. Tahreen et al. [ 43 ] reported a similar pattern in compression, where UCS increased significantly between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹ and then levelled off towards 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. Afrin et al. [ 45 ] observed analogous behaviour in a friction stir-welded workpiece, attributing the rate sensitivity of UCS to the combined effect of work-hardening and delayed activation of damage mechanisms at higher rates.

The magnitude of UCS in the present WAAM wall (1.9 to 2.1 times the yield strength based on mean values; Table  4 ) is typical of ductile low-carbon steels in compression, where substantial post-yield hardening is accommodated by distributed dislocation slip and micro-buckling of ferrite plates before macroscopic instability. Compared with wrought low-carbon steels with a similar composition, the WAAM material performed at least comparably despite its heterogeneous as-built microstructure. This suggests that the refined interlayer ferritic grains and high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) (Fig.  5 ) provide sufficient barriers to dislocation motion and support stable compressive hardening.

Where σ UCS  and σ YS  are the ultimate compressive strength and 0.2% offset yield strength, respectively. Physically, Hc measures the extent to which the material can harden relative to its yield strength; Hc = 0 indicates perfectly plastic behaviour, whereas higher values reflect strong strain hardening.

In Fig.  8 (c), Hc for the WAAM wall lies between 0.93 and 1.15. Specifically, at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, Hc 0.93 ± 0.14, increases slightly to 1.00 ± 0.13 at 10⁻³ s⁻¹, peaks at 1.15 ± 0.15 at 10⁻² s⁻¹, and then decreases to 0.99 ± 0.05 at 10⁻¹ s⁻¹. The overall picture is that the wall exhibits substantial ability to harden after yielding, with the most pronounced hardening at an intermediate strain rate. Tahreen et al. [ 43 ] reported Hc 1.0-1.4 for cast Mg-Al alloys, also with a maximum around 10⁻² s⁻¹. They related this to the competition between dislocation multiplication and dynamic recovery: at very low rates, recovery lowers Hc; at very high rates, the onset of localised deformation and microcracking can cap Hc. Similar Hc levels have been reported for heterogeneous Al-Si alloys and high-strength steels under compression, where the presence of multiple phases and high dislocation storage capacity promotes sustained hardening up to large strains [ 44 ,  46 ]. The present WAAM ER70S-6 wall fits within this envelope, suggesting that the refined ferrite-pearlite matrix and HAGB-rich grain-boundary network contribute to sustained post-yield hardening during compression.

The slight drop in Hc at 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ may indicate the earlier localisation or reduced additional hardening before instability. This is consistent with the stress-strain curves in Fig.  7 , where the highest-rate curve shows a slightly shorter plateau before densification compared with 10⁻² s⁻¹.

The initial purpose of these equations was to represent uniform work-hardening prior to necking under tension. However, subsequent research has demonstrated their applicability in describing the compression behaviour of cast magnesium alloys, heterostructured aluminium alloys, and advanced steels across a broad range of strain rates [ 43 ,  44 ,  45 – 46 ].

The compressive flow curves of the Hollomon, Ludwik, Swift, and Afrin models showed limited variation with strain rate, suggesting that a single rate‑dependent parameter set can be used to capture the quasi‑static compressive response of the circular WAAM ER70S‑6 wall in numerical simulations. The Hollomon strength coefficient K and hardening exponent n showed limited variation across strain rates, indicating that the underlying deformation mechanisms (HAGB strengthening) remained stable in the quasi-static regime. This behaviour aligns with the high Hc values (Table  4 ) and the HAGB-dominated microstructure (Fig.  5 ), and is consistent with WAAM low-carbon steels exhibiting sustained work hardening under monotonic loading.

sections.heading: Structure-property relationships for the WAAM circular wall
paragraphs: The integration of SEM, EBSD, hardness, and compression results provides a comprehensive understanding of how the as-built microstructure of the circular WAAM wall influences its quasi-static compressive behaviour. In the context of the deposit scale, the circular wall was composed of five superimposed beads, each maintaining a relatively consistent height of approximately 2 mm (total height 10 mm) and a local width of approximately 10 mm. This structure displays a ferrite-pearlite matrix, characterised by the presence of scattered gas pores within the central wall region, alongside a coarser fusion zone (FZ) located at the interface between the wall and substrate, as shown in Figs.  3  and  4  [ 22 ,  30 ,  31 ]. The analysis of the EBSD cube and misorientation at the centre of the wall indicated a heterogeneous grain boundary network predominantly consisting of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). Specifically, approximately 28% of the boundaries were classified as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs, 2–15°), whereas approximately 72% were high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, > 15°). The misorientation histogram exhibits peaks at 2–5° and 30–55° range (Fig.  5 ). The HAGB-rich topology aligns with previous WAAM studies on ER70S-6 and similar low-carbon steel. In these studies, rapid solidification, accompanied by multiple reheating cycles, facilitated recovery and recrystallisation, resulting in the transformation of the initial subgrain structures into fine equiaxed ferrite delineated by HAGBs [ 52 ,  53 ].

The hardness profile observed in the wall-substrate cross-section (Fig.  6 ) indicates the presence of microstructural heterogeneity. In the upper and mid-wall regions, where the SEM and EBSD images show refined ferrite-pearlite with a relatively uniform grain size, the hardness mostly remains within approximately 200–235 HV, with local peaks approaching 240–250 HV. This level is similar to those of other ER70S-6 WAAM deposits constructed on structural steel or stainless steel substrates, which generally exhibit hardness values of 200–260 HV in ferrite-pearlite regions [ 21 ,  22 ,  54 ]. The hardness at the wall-substrate interface exhibited a distinct minimum of approximately 100–150 HV within the fusion-boundary region. This is succeeded by a gradual increase to around 190–220 HV in the partially melted zone (PMZ), heat-affected zone (HAZ), and substrate. Similar “soft FZ” profiles have been documented for WAAM ER70S-6/316L and ER70S-6/S355 bimetal structures. These profiles are attributed to dilution-induced alterations in the carbon and alloying contents, along with coarsened ferrite grains and decreased dislocation density in the initial layers [ 54 ,  55 ]. In the present circular wall, the relatively narrow extent of this soft fusion-boundary region and the recovery of hardness in the HAZ/substrate indicate that the low-strength region is geometrically confined, which is important for the overall compressive stability of the ring-like component.

The macroscopic compressive response, as illustrated in Figs.  7  and  8 , closely aligned with the observed microstructure and hardness distribution. At strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, the mean 0.2% compressive yield strength (YS) derived from the true stress-strain curves was observed to be 368.3 ± 20.2 to 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa, whereas the mean ultimate compressive strength (UCS) was recorded between 729.0 ± 31.2 to 801.7 ± 56.2 MPa (Fig.  8 (a, b), Table  4 ). The mean compressive YS values are lower than the nominal tensile strength of the ER70S-6 wire (approximately 480 MPa in tension; Table  2 ). In contrast, the UCS values exceed the nominal wire tensile strength. The high UCS values reflect strong post-yield hardening under compression. Additionally, these values are comparable to, or higher than, ultimate strengths reported for rectilinear ER70S-6 WAAM walls and bimetal joints following moderate heat input processing [ 56 ,  57 ]. In the studies conducted, yield strength (YS) values ranging from approximately 330 to 380 MPa and ultimate strengths between approximately 600 and 750 MPa have been linked to ferrite-pearlite matrices exhibiting comparable hardness levels of 200 to 250 HV [ 22 ,  31 ]. These results indicate that the current circular wall attains at least equivalent strength, and in certain instances, superior strength, even though it is produced through a more geometrically intricate process.

The significant proportion of HAGBs present in the centre of the wall can explain the observed yield and work-hardening behaviour. In ferrite-pearlite steels, the density of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGB) is known to improve strength through mechanisms of grain-boundary strengthening and enhanced storage of geometrically necessary dislocations. This phenomenon also contributes to a more uniform plastic flow and delays the onset of localisation [ 52 ,  53 ,  58 ,  59 ]. Quantitative studies on low-carbon and HSLA steels indicate that an increase in the HAGB fraction beyond approximately 60% at a constant grain size can elevate the yield strength by 30–70 MPa and enhance the strain-hardening exponent n by approximately 0.05–0.1 [ 22 ]. The current wall microstructure, comprising approximately 72% HAGBs and exhibiting a hardness of about 200–235 HV in the EBSD sampling area, is categorised within the strengthened regime. This classification aligns with the observed yield strength of 368–397 MPa at intermediate strain rates, as well as the Ludwik n values ranging from 0.46 to 0.59, which were obtained from the true stress-true plastic strain curves (Fig.  8 (d)). Similar combinations of elevated HAGB fractions, moderate hardness, and significant work hardening have been observed in WAAM-fabricated ER70S-6 low-carbon steel blocks and ER70S-6-based graded structures under quasi-static loading conditions [ 22 ,  55 ]. Furthermore, the uniform hardness (200–235 HV) in the mid-wall region, from which the compression specimens were extracted, correlates well with the high YS and UCS values reported in Table  4  and the sustained work hardening observed in the stress-strain curves.

Qualitatively observed gas pores represent one local microstructural heterogeneity in the deposited wall. The SEM image of the wall centre in Fig.  4  shows isolated pores and limited local clustering within the examined field. Previous studies on WAAM ER70S-6 and carbon-steel deposits have shown that pores, voids, and other microstructural imperfections can reduce mechanical or fatigue performance when their size, density, or location is unfavourable [ 22 ,  31 ,  57 ]. In the present work, pore size, pore density, and pore area fraction were not quantified. Therefore, pores are treated qualitatively. The smooth compression curves in Fig.  7  and the hardening response in Fig.  8  are interpreted mainly through the HAGB-rich ferrite-pearlite matrix, the measured hardness profile, and the compressive flow behaviour.

The circular geometry and loading configuration introduce an additional dimension to the structure-property relationship. The compression specimens were machined cylinders with dimensions of 4 mm in diameter and 6 mm in height, sourced from the mid-height of the circular wall. The morphology of the as-built ring significantly affects the thermal history, cooling rates, and consequently, the microstructure and residual stresses present in the material. In circular toolpaths, heat accumulation occurs near the inner radius, whereas the outer region experiences more rapid cooling. This may promote subtle radial gradients in grain size, thermal history, and defect distribution, which can be less pronounced in straight-wall WAAM builds [ 60 ,  61 ]. Experimental and numerical investigations on ring and collar components manufactured using arc-based and laser-based additive manufacturing have demonstrated circumferential heat accumulation. This heat accumulation can result in marginally elevated hardness and strength in the inner wall. Additionally, this phenomenon contributes to an increase in residual hoop compression, thereby enhancing the compressive load-bearing capacity under conditions that simulate service environments [ 22 ,  62 ]. The relatively isotropic EBSD orientation distribution and the absence of strong texture in the present wall (Fig.  5 (a, b)) indicate that any such gradients are modest; combined with the HAGB-rich network, this suggests that the circular WAAM ring is unlikely to suffer from severe anisotropy in compressive response around the circumference.

The integrated analysis of microstructure, hardness, and compressive strength presents significant implications for the design of WAAM-fabricated rings, collars, and analogous tubular components. First, the present results indicate that an HAGB-rich ferrite-pearlite microstructure and a relatively uniform hardness profile in the deposited wall are sufficient to support compressive strengths exceeding 700 MPa at room temperature without post-processing in the investigated circular WAAM wall. Second, it is essential to carefully control the heat input during the initial layers to restrict the width and softness of the fusion zone (FZ). Failure to do so may result in the wall-substrate interface becoming the limiting factor for compressive stiffness and buckling resistance, as reported in other bimetal and graded-steel WAAM systems [ 22 ,  54 ]. The results obtained in this study show that walls made by circular WAAM with a similar microstructure can resist quasi-static compressive loads with a small variation in strength. This is promising for applications such as load transfer collars, bearing housings, and stiffening rings in welded structures, where the loading rate can vary.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The feasibility and performance of the circular WAAM ER70S-6 wall deposited on SS400 steel were investigated, and the relationships between the microstructure, hardness distribution, and compressive properties at various quasi-static strain rates were analysed. The conclusions drawn from this study are presented below.

SEM and EBSD revealed a predominantly ferritic-pearlitic matrix in the wall, with an HAGB fraction of 72% and a mixed misorientation spectrum characteristic of recovered and recrystallised ferrite. Microhardness in the load-bearing region of the wall was relatively uniform at 200–235 HV, whereas a narrow coarse-grained fusion-boundary region at the wall-substrate interface exhibited a hardness dip to 100–150 HV. Under quasi-static compression at strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, the circular wall exhibited 0.2% yield strengths of 368.3 ± 20.2 to 397.0 ± 2.6 MPa and ultimate compressive strengths of 729.0 ± 31.2 to 801.7 ± 56.2 MPa, that is, approximately two times the yield strength. Both YS and UCS showed only modest increases with strain rate, corresponding to a small strain-rate sensitivity, indicating that the ferrite-pearlite WAAM microstructure delivers a stable compressive response. The circular WAAM ER70S-6 wall showed strong work hardening (0.93–1.15) after yielding, and this trend was consistently captured by the constitutive models: Hollomon, Ludwik, Swift, and Afrin, used to fit the compressive flow curves. Together with the HAGB-dominated ferrite-pearlite microstructure, relatively uniform hardness in the load-bearing region, and geometrically confined soft fusion zone at the interface, this behaviour indicates that the as-built circular wall can sustain high compressive loads while absorbing substantial plastic energy. These structure-property features suggest clear process levers for designing WAAM-fabricated rings, collars, and similar circular components that achieve reliable compressive performance.
